cards.title: Vertex AI — The Unified ML Platform
cards.teaser: Vertex AI is Google Cloud's umbrella service for everything machine learning: it unifies model training, evaluation, deployment, serving, and monitoring under one API surface — so you do not have to stitch together separate services as a workload matures.

runs.text: Before Vertex AI (launched 2021), GCP ML tooling was fragmented: AI Platform for training, Cloud ML Engine for serving, AutoML products scattered across products, and no shared concept of a model registry or pipeline. Vertex AI consolidated all of this under a single SDK, a single IAM surface, and a single Cloud Console section.
The key concepts Vertex AI introduces:

items.text: Model Registry
— versioned store for trained models, regardless of how they were trained (custom training, AutoML, imported).
Endpoints
— managed serving infrastructure; deploy one or more model versions to an endpoint and split traffic between them.
Datasets
— managed dataset objects that link training data to experiments for reproducibility.
Experiments
— run tracking that records hyperparameters, metrics, and artifacts across training runs.
Feature Store
— centralized feature repository that eliminates training-serving skew by sharing the same feature computation between offline training and online inference.

runs.text: A minimal Python SDK interaction looks like this:

explanation.text:
from google.cloud import aiplatform

aiplatform.init(project="my-project", location="us-central1")

# List all models in the registry
for model in aiplatform.Model.list():
    print(model.display_name, model.version_id)

runs.text: Vertex AI bills are per-component: training node-hours, prediction compute, storage, and pipeline orchestration are priced separately. The unified console hides this complexity, but budget alerts should be set per product family.
Vertex AI is the one roof under which GCP puts all ML work — training, serving, pipelines, registries, and monitoring — so you don't have to wire together a dozen separate services yourself.

cards.title: Model Garden — Pre-Trained Models on Demand
cards.teaser: Model Garden is the Vertex AI catalogue of pre-trained models — from Google's own Gemini family to open-source heavyweights like Llama and Mistral — accessible via a single API without managing infrastructure or downloading weights.

runs.text: Model Garden solves the problem of model procurement: finding a model, verifying its licence, deploying it at scale, and keeping it available. It provides three categories of models:

items.text: Google first-party models
— the Gemini family (Pro, Flash, Nano), PaLM 2 legacy variants, Imagen, Veo, Embeddings APIs, and Chirp (speech).
Open-source models (Google-hosted)
— Meta's Llama family, Mistral, Gemma (Google's open-weight model), and community fine-tunes. These deploy to Vertex AI-managed infrastructure; you call an endpoint, not a self-hosted server.
Partner and third-party models
— models from Anthropic, AI21 Labs, and Cohere available through the same Vertex AI endpoint pattern.

runs.text: Deploying a Model Garden model to a Vertex AI endpoint:

explanation.text:
from google.cloud import aiplatform

aiplatform.init(project="my-project", location="us-central1")

# Deploy Llama 3 from Model Garden
model = aiplatform.Model(model_name="publishers/meta/models/llama-3-8b-instruct-hf-001")

endpoint = model.deploy(
    machine_type="g2-standard-12",
    accelerator_type="NVIDIA_L4",
    accelerator_count=1
)

response = endpoint.predict(instances=[{"prompt": "Explain gradient descent."}])
print(response.predictions[0])

runs.text: When evaluating Model Garden entries, look for the model card's benchmark scores on your target task, not headline parameter counts. A 7B model fine-tuned on domain data routinely outperforms a 70B general model on narrow tasks.
Model Garden is an app store for ML models — Google's own, plus popular open-source ones — all deployable through the same Vertex AI endpoint API, no weight-downloading or GPU wrangling required.

cards.title: Gemini APIs — Pro, Flash, and Nano Compared
cards.teaser: Gemini is Google's frontier LLM family. Pro, Flash, and Nano are not just size variants — they represent different cost/capability/latency trade-offs optimised for different deployment contexts: cloud reasoning, cloud speed, and on-device respectively.

runs.text: All three Gemini variants share the same multimodal architecture (text, image, audio, video, code) but are trained and distilled for different operating points. The right choice depends on the problem, not on brand preference.

items.text: Gemini Pro

— highest capability in the cloud tier. Best for complex reasoning, long-context understanding (up to 1M tokens context window on some versions), code generation, multi-step agentic tasks. Highest latency and cost per token. Choose Pro when quality is the constraint.
Gemini Flash

— optimised for speed and cost, not raw capability. Significantly lower latency and price than Pro, with acceptable quality for most summarisation, classification, retrieval-augmented generation, and chatbot tasks. Choose Flash when throughput or cost is the constraint.
Gemini Nano

— distilled for on-device inference (Android, Pixel hardware). Not available via the Vertex AI cloud API in the same way as Pro/Flash; accessed through the Gemini Nano on-device SDK. Choose Nano for privacy-sensitive or offline mobile tasks.

runs.text: Calling Gemini Pro via the Vertex AI SDK:

explanation.text:
import vertexai
from vertexai.generative_models import GenerativeModel

vertexai.init(project="my-project", location="us-central1")

# Switch model_name to "gemini-1.5-flash" for the Flash variant
model = GenerativeModel("gemini-1.5-pro")

response = model.generate_content(
    "Summarise the CAP theorem in three sentences.",
    generation_config={"temperature": 0.2, "max_output_tokens": 256}
)
print(response.text)

runs.text: Gemini model version strings change frequently (e.g. gemini-1.5-pro vs gemini-2.0-pro). Frame evaluations around the Pro/Flash/Nano tier rather than specific version strings — pin to a dated alias (gemini-1.5-pro-002) in production to avoid unexpected behaviour changes on model upgrades.

Pro is the powerful cloud model for hard problems; Flash is the fast, cheap cloud model for high-volume tasks; Nano runs on device when you can't send data to the cloud. Same family, different trade-offs.

cards.title: Vertex AI Workbench — Managed Jupyter Notebooks
cards.teaser: Vertex AI Workbench provides managed Jupyter notebook instances pre-configured with ML libraries, GCP SDK integrations, and IAM-controlled access — eliminating the overhead of provisioning and maintaining notebook infrastructure.

runs.text: Workbench comes in two modes, which represent different management trade-offs:

items.text: Managed notebooks (Workbench Instances)

— Google manages the underlying VM, applies security patches, and provides idle shutdown to control cost. You get a JupyterLab interface attached to a Compute Engine instance with a service account for GCP access.
User-managed notebooks (legacy)
— full control over the VM configuration, CUDA versions, and custom containers. Higher maintenance overhead; prefer Workbench Instances for new projects.

runs.text: Key Workbench features to evaluate:

items.text: Scheduled notebooks
— run a notebook on a cron schedule via Vertex AI Pipelines, useful for recurring data analysis or model evaluation reports.
Git integration
— built-in JupyterLab Git extension connects to Cloud Source Repositories or GitHub for version control.
Executor
— submit a notebook for headless execution on a separate Vertex AI job, separating interactive authoring from batch compute.
GPU selection
— attach T4, L4, A100, or H100 GPUs; the machine type is configurable at instance creation and changeable on stop.

runs.text: Workbench instances bill for the underlying Compute Engine VM even when the notebook is idle. Always configure the idle-shutdown policy (typically 30-60 minutes) or use the Executor for long-running jobs rather than leaving a notebook kernel running overnight.
Workbench is Jupyter in the cloud with GCP plumbing already set up — IAM, GPU, storage access — so you start experimenting in minutes instead of configuring infrastructure.

cards.title: Vertex AI Pipelines — Kubeflow-Based ML Workflows
cards.teaser: Vertex AI Pipelines is a managed orchestrator for reproducible ML workflows: each step runs in an isolated container, artifacts are tracked automatically, and the full pipeline is versioned and auditable — solving the "works on my notebook" problem at production scale.

runs.text: Vertex AI Pipelines is built on Kubeflow Pipelines (KFP) v2. Pipelines are defined in Python using the KFP SDK, compiled to a platform-agnostic YAML/JSON IR (Intermediate Representation), and submitted to Vertex for execution. Each step ("component") runs in its own container on managed infrastructure.
A minimal pipeline definition:
Key capabilities to evaluate:

items.text: Artifact lineage
— Vertex ML Metadata automatically records inputs and outputs of every component, enabling root-cause analysis when model quality degrades.
Caching
— component outputs are cached by input fingerprint; re-running a pipeline after a single-step change skips unchanged upstream steps.
Scheduled runs
— pipelines can be triggered on a cron schedule for regular retraining.

runs.text: Vertex AI Pipelines is charged per pipeline step execution minute, not per pipeline. Design components to be granular enough for caching benefits but not so fine-grained that orchestration overhead dominates. A good rule of thumb: each component should take at least 30 seconds to run.
Pipelines turns a sequence of ML steps — preprocess, train, evaluate, deploy — into a versioned, replayable workflow where every input, output, and metric is tracked automatically.

cards.title: AutoML — No-Code Model Training
cards.teaser: AutoML lets you train a production-quality model from labelled data without writing training code — Vertex AI handles architecture search, hyperparameter tuning, and deployment. The trade-off is less customisation for significantly less engineering effort.

runs.text: AutoML covers four data modalities, each with its own supported task types:

items.text: Tabular

— binary/multi-class classification, regression, forecasting. Suitable for structured business data (churn, pricing, demand). Uses an ensemble of gradient boosting and neural architectures selected via NAS.
Image
— image classification, object detection, segmentation. Transfer-learns from Google's internal vision models; achieves competitive accuracy with a few hundred labelled images.
Text
— text classification, sentiment analysis, entity extraction. Fine-tunes on BERT-family models.
Video
— video classification, action recognition, object tracking.

explanation.text:
from google.cloud import aiplatform

aiplatform.init(project="my-project", location="us-central1")

# Create a tabular dataset from BigQuery
dataset = aiplatform.TabularDataset.create(
    display_name="churn-dataset",
    bq_source="bq://my-project.my-dataset.churn_table"
)

# Train an AutoML model
job = aiplatform.AutoMLTabularTrainingJob(
    display_name="churn-automl",
    optimization_prediction_type="classification"
)

model = job.run(
    dataset=dataset,
    target_column="churned",
    budget_milli_node_hours=1000
)

runs.text: AutoML is worth evaluating before reaching for custom training — it often achieves 80-90% of the performance of a hand-tuned model in a fraction of the time. Use it to establish a quality baseline; switch to custom training only when AutoML hits a ceiling that matters for your use case.
AutoML is the "give me your labelled data and I'll give you a deployed model" path — no ML expertise needed, and often good enough that you never need to write a training loop.

cards.title: Vertex AI Search — RAG-as-a-Service
cards.teaser: Vertex AI Search (formerly Enterprise Search on Gen App Builder) is Google's managed retrieval-augmented generation service: you point it at your documents or data stores, and it returns grounded answers with citations — without you building a RAG pipeline from scratch.

runs.text: The core problem Vertex AI Search solves: building a production RAG pipeline requires a document ingestion pipeline, a chunking strategy, an embedding model, a vector store, a retrieval layer, a reranker, and a generation step — each requiring tuning and maintenance. Vertex AI Search bundles all of this into a managed API.
Supported data store types:

items.text: Unstructured documents
— PDFs, HTML, DOCX uploaded to Cloud Storage or crawled from a website. Vertex AI handles parsing, chunking, and embedding.
Structured data
— BigQuery tables or JSON records; enables SQL-backed retrieval grounded with semantic search.
Website corpus
— provide a domain and Vertex AI crawls and indexes it, useful for customer-facing search on documentation sites.
Third-party connectors
— pre-built connectors for Confluence, Google Drive, Jira, Salesforce, and others.

runs.text: Querying a Vertex AI Search app with grounded generation:

explanation.text:
from google.cloud import discoveryengine_v1 as discoveryengine

client = discoveryengine.SearchServiceClient()

request = discoveryengine.SearchRequest(
    serving_config=(
        "projects/my-project/locations/global/collections/default_collection"
        "/dataStores/my-datastore/servingConfigs/default_serving_config"
    ),
    query="What is our refund policy for digital products?",
    page_size=5,
    content_search_spec=discoveryengine.SearchRequest.ContentSearchSpec(
        summary_spec=discoveryengine.SearchRequest.ContentSearchSpec.SummarySpec(
            summary_result_count=3,
            include_citations=True
        )
    )
)

response = client.search(request)
print(response.summary.summary_text)

runs.text: Real-world use cases: internal knowledge base search for support agents (reduces handle time), regulatory document Q&A for compliance teams, product catalogue search with semantic understanding, and code documentation search. The citation feature is critical for enterprise trust — users need to verify answers against source documents.

Vertex AI Search is RAG as a managed service — you give it your documents, it handles the indexing, retrieval, and answer generation, and returns cited answers without you needing to build or maintain the pipeline.

cards.title: Embeddings APIs — Text and Multimodal
cards.teaser: Vertex AI's Embeddings APIs convert text, images, or video into dense vector representations suitable for semantic search, clustering, classification, and retrieval — without training your own embedding model.

runs.text: Embeddings are the foundation of modern semantic applications. Instead of matching on keywords, you compare vectors in a high-dimensional space — close vectors mean similar meaning. Vertex AI provides two embedding model families:

items.text: text-embedding-gecko / text-embedding-004

— text-only embeddings, producing 768-dimensional vectors. Optimised for retrieval tasks (asymmetric: short query vs longer document) and symmetric similarity tasks. The task_type parameter lets you specify RETRIEVAL_QUERY, RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT, SEMANTIC_SIMILARITY, or CLASSIFICATION.
multimodalembedding
— embeds text, images, and video clips into a shared 1408-dimensional space, enabling cross-modal retrieval: find images matching a text description, or text captions matching an image.

explanation.text:
from vertexai.language_models import TextEmbeddingModel

model = TextEmbeddingModel.from_pretrained("text-embedding-004")

# task_type directs the model to optimise for retrieval
embeddings = model.get_embeddings(
    ["How do I reset my password?"],
    task_type="RETRIEVAL_QUERY"
)

print(len(embeddings[0].values))  # 768

# For multimodal:
from vertexai.vision_models import MultiModalEmbeddingModel, Image

mm_model = MultiModalEmbeddingModel.from_pretrained("multimodalembedding@001")
result = mm_model.get_embeddings(
    image=Image.load_from_file("product.jpg"),
    contextual_text="red running shoe"
)

runs.text: The task_type parameter on text embeddings is easy to overlook and has measurable impact on retrieval quality. Always specify RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT when embedding your corpus and RETRIEVAL_QUERY when embedding the user query — the asymmetric training improves recall by 5-15% in typical benchmarks.

Embeddings APIs turn words, sentences, or images into numbers (vectors) that capture meaning — similar content gets similar numbers, which makes semantic search and clustering possible without any training.

cards.title: Vector Search — Managed ANN at Scale
cards.teaser: Vertex AI Vector Search (formerly Matching Engine) is a managed approximate nearest-neighbour service that finds the most similar vectors to a query in milliseconds — even across billion-scale corpora — without managing index infrastructure.

runs.text: The problem it solves: once you have embeddings, you need to find the K nearest neighbours of a query vector efficiently. Brute-force cosine search is O(n) in the corpus size. For a million-document corpus, this takes seconds; for a billion-item catalogue, it is unusable. Vector Search uses ANN (Approximate Nearest Neighbour) algorithms — specifically, a tree-based and graph-based hybrid — to return results in single-digit milliseconds at billion scale.
The workflow:

items.text: Create an index
— upload your embedding vectors (JSON or CSV in Cloud Storage) and Vertex builds the ANN index. Choose between streaming updates (for corpora that change frequently) and batch updates.
Deploy the index to an IndexEndpoint
— an IndexEndpoint is a VPC-backed serving node; deploy one or more indexes to it and query them via gRPC or REST.
Query
— send a query vector, receive the K nearest neighbours with their distances and datapoint IDs.

explanation.text:
from google.cloud import aiplatform

aiplatform.init(project="my-project", location="us-central1")

my_index_endpoint = aiplatform.MatchingEngineIndexEndpoint(
    index_endpoint_name="projects/my-project/locations/us-central1"
                         "/indexEndpoints/1234567890"
)

response = my_index_endpoint.find_neighbors(
    deployed_index_id="my_deployed_index",
    queries=[[0.1, 0.25, 0.8, ...]],  # query embedding vector
    num_neighbors=10
)

for match in response[0]:
    print(match.id, match.distance)

runs.text: Vector Search supports filtering: you can attach metadata to each datapoint (e.g., document_type, language, date) and combine ANN retrieval with a filter predicate. This narrows the search space before ANN runs, which is more efficient than post-filtering results.
Vector Search is the managed index that answers "which of my million embeddings is closest to this query vector?" in milliseconds — it's what makes semantic search fast enough for production use.

cards.title: AI Agent Builder — Agentic Workflows
cards.teaser: Vertex AI Agent Builder provides managed infrastructure for building multi-step, tool-using agents: it handles the orchestration loop, tool calling, memory, and grounding, so you define the tools and goals rather than the plumbing.

runs.text: AI Agent Builder (part of the Vertex AI Agent Builder product family, formerly Dialogflow CX for structured flows) targets production agentic applications. The key capability it adds over calling Gemini directly is
managed tool execution and state
across multi-turn interactions.

items.text: Tools
— define OpenAPI-spec functions; the agent calls them when the LLM decides it needs external data. Tools can call Cloud Functions, Cloud Run services, or third-party APIs.
Data stores
— connect Vertex AI Search data stores for grounded retrieval; the agent queries the search app as a tool.
Session memory
— managed session state persists context across multi-turn conversations without you managing a session store.
Evaluation
— built-in evaluation framework to measure agent trajectory quality, tool call accuracy, and response groundedness.

explanation.text:
from vertexai.preview.reasoning_engines import LangchainAgent
import vertexai

vertexai.init(project="my-project", location="us-central1")

# Define tools
def get_order_status(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Returns the status of an order given its ID."""
    # Call internal order service here
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped"}

agent = LangchainAgent(
    model="gemini-1.5-pro",
    tools=[get_order_status],
    model_kwargs={"temperature": 0}
)

remote_agent = agent.deploy(
    requirements=["google-cloud-aiplatform"],
    display_name="order-support-agent"
)

response = remote_agent.query(input="Where is order #12345?")
print(response["output"])

runs.text: Agentic applications are harder to evaluate than single-turn completions — a correct final answer can be reached via a wrong tool trajectory. Use Agent Builder's evaluation framework to assess trajectory quality, not just output quality. Track tool call precision and recall separately from answer quality.
AI Agent Builder is the managed scaffold for agents that need to call tools, remember context across turns, and search your data — you write the tools and goals; it runs the reasoning loop.

cards.title: Document AI — OCR and Form Extraction
cards.teaser: Document AI converts unstructured documents — PDFs, images, scanned forms — into structured data using specialised processors for OCR, form parsing, and domain-specific extraction: invoices, contracts, tax forms, ID documents.

runs.text: Document AI solves a different problem than general-purpose LLMs applied to documents: it provides high-precision structural extraction (bounding boxes, field labels, values, tables, signatures) suitable for downstream automation, not conversational interaction.
Processor types available in Document AI:

items.text: Document OCR
— general-purpose OCR with layout detection (paragraphs, tables, columns). Multilingual; supports handwriting.
Form Parser
— extracts key-value pairs from forms without knowing the form schema in advance; uses visual layout to pair labels with values.
Specialized parsers

— Invoice Parser, Expense Parser, W2/1099 Parser, Bank Statement Parser, Contract Document Understanding, Identity Document Parser (passports, driving licences). Each is trained on domain-specific layouts.
Custom Document Extractor
— train a custom processor on your own document schema using Workbench labelling; uses foundation model fine-tuning rather than rules.

runs.text: Evaluate Document AI on your actual document corpus before choosing between a specialized parser and a custom extractor. Specialized parsers achieve 90%+ field accuracy on well-formed standard documents but degrade on non-standard layouts; custom extractors require labelling effort but generalise to your specific document variants.
Document AI reads your PDFs and scanned forms and pulls out structured data — "invoice total: $1,250" as a typed field, not as raw text — using processors trained on the specific document type.

cards.title: Discrete AI APIs — Vision, Speech, and Translation
cards.teaser: GCP's discrete AI APIs — Vision AI, Speech-to-Text, Text-to-Speech, Natural Language API, and Translation API — are single-purpose, REST-callable inference services for common perception tasks, requiring no training and no model management.

runs.text: These APIs predate Vertex AI and remain the simplest path when you need a well-defined perception capability without the overhead of managing models or pipelines:

items.text: Vision AI

— label detection, object localisation, safe search detection, logo detection, facial detection, landmark recognition, text detection (OCR), and image properties. Accessible via the Cloud Vision API; one API call returns a structured JSON response with all detected features.
Speech-to-Text

— transcribes audio in 125+ languages, with speaker diarisation, word-level timestamps, and custom vocabulary (for domain-specific terms). The v2 API (Chirp model) significantly improves accuracy on accented and noisy speech.
Text-to-Speech
— synthesises natural speech from text using WaveNet and Neural2 voices; supports SSML for pronunciation control.
Natural Language API
— entity extraction, sentiment analysis, content classification, and syntax analysis on text.
Translation API
— text and document translation across 100+ languages, with glossary support for domain-specific terminology preservation.

runs.text: Evaluate the discrete APIs against Gemini for your use case before assuming newer is better. Vision AI label detection is faster and cheaper than prompting Gemini with an image for simple classification tasks. Use Gemini when you need reasoning or language output alongside perception; use the discrete APIs when you need structured, typed perception results at high throughput.

The discrete AI APIs are specialised one-trick ponies — Vision recognises objects, Speech transcribes audio, Translation converts language — all available as a single REST call with no model management.

cards.title: Generative Media — Imagen and Veo
cards.teaser: Imagen generates high-quality images from text prompts; Veo generates video. Both are accessible via the Vertex AI SDK and represent Google's generative media capabilities — useful for content creation workflows, product visualisation, and synthetic training data.

runs.text: Imagen and Veo are diffusion-based generative models available through Vertex AI. They are distinct from Gemini (which is primarily a language and multimodal understanding model) — their task is media generation, not conversation or reasoning.

items.text: Imagen

— text-to-image generation, image editing (inpainting, outpainting), image upscaling, and visual question answering about generated images. Supports style transfer and subject fine-tuning ("generate product images in a consistent style").
Veo

— text-to-video and image-to-video generation. Produces short video clips (typically 5-30 seconds) at up to 4K resolution. Camera motion controls (zoom, pan, tracking shot) are specified in the prompt.

explanation.text:
from vertexai.preview.vision_models import ImageGenerationModel

model = ImageGenerationModel.from_pretrained("imagegeneration@006")

response = model.generate_images(
    prompt="A photorealistic image of a red ceramic mug on a wooden desk, soft morning light, depth of field",
    number_of_images=4,
    aspect_ratio="1:1",
    safety_filter_level="block_some",
    person_generation="dont_allow"
)

for i, image in enumerate(response.images):
    image.save(f"output_{i}.png")

runs.text: Both Imagen and Veo embed SynthID watermarks in generated media — a cryptographic signal that survives compression, cropping, and social media re-encoding. This is useful for provenance tracking in enterprise content workflows but should be disclosed to end users in consumer-facing applications. Review Google's usage policies before deploying generative media in production; prohibited use cases (e.g. realistic depictions of real people) are enforced at the API level.

Imagen turns a text description into an image; Veo turns it into a video. Both are available through the same Vertex AI SDK, and both watermark their outputs with SynthID so you can prove what was machine-generated.
